questions.prompt: What happens when this program reaches the end of `main`?
options: The destructor of `t` joins the thread, and the program exits normally
The destructor of `t` detaches the thread, and the program exits normally
Undefined behavior
`std::terminate` is called
questions.explanation: `t` is still joinable when it is destroyed, because nobody called `join()` or `detach()`. [thread.thread.destr] specifies that destroying a joinable `std::thread` calls `std::terminate`, so this is well-defined termination rather than undefined behavior. Implicit joining is what `std::jthread` does; `std::thread` deliberately refuses to pick either policy for you.

options: Well-formed, and `x` is 1 after the join
Well-formed, but `inc` increments a copy, so `x` stays 0
Ill-formed: the decay-copied argument is an rvalue and cannot bind to `int&`
Undefined behavior: data race on `x`
questions.explanation: The thread constructor decay-copies each argument in the calling thread and passes the copies to the function as rvalues. An rvalue `int` cannot bind to `int&`, so the constructor's requirement that the call be invocable fails and the program does not compile. The second option describes what happens for a `const int&` parameter. Passing `std::ref(x)` makes it compile and increment `x` itself.

questions.prompt: In C++20, what does this program do?
options: Prints `main done`, then `stopped`, and exits normally
Calls `std::terminate`, because `t` is joinable when destroyed
Hangs forever, because nothing calls `request_stop`
Prints `main done` and exits; the loop is killed with the process
questions.explanation: `std::jthread` passes its own stop token to a callable whose first parameter is a `std::stop_token`. Its destructor calls `request_stop()` and then `join()`, so the loop sees the request, prints `stopped`, and the join returns. Termination on a joinable destructor is the `std::thread` rule, which `jthread` replaces, and the hang would only happen if the destructor joined without requesting stop.

options: It is safe: the `std::string` is built from `buf` before the constructor returns
It is ill-formed: a `char` array cannot be passed to a `const std::string&` parameter
It is safe because `detach` waits until the arguments have been consumed
The new thread may build the string from a dangling `char*` after `start` returns, which is undefined behavior
questions.explanation: Decay-copying applies to the argument as written, so the thread stores a copy of the `char*` that `buf` decays to. The conversion to `std::string` happens when the new thread calls `show`, which may be after `start` has returned and `buf` is gone. Converting at the call site, as `std::string(buf)`, makes the string itself the stored copy. The first option is what most people assume, but the constructor only copies; it never applies the parameter's conversion.

options: Prints `caught`, because `join` rethrows the thread's exception
Prints `caught`, because the exception unwinds into the creating thread
Calls `std::terminate`; `caught` is never printed
Undefined behavior
questions.explanation: [thread.thread.constr] says that if the thread's function exits with an uncaught exception, `std::terminate` is called. Exceptions do not cross thread boundaries, and `join` has no channel to carry one. Rethrowing on retrieval is what `std::future::get` does, which is the tempting confusion. To report errors, catch in the thread and pass a `std::exception_ptr` or use a promise.

questions.prompt: In C++20, what does this program print?
options: `1 1`, and the callback never runs because it was registered too late
`callback` then `1 0`
`1 0` then `callback`, printed when `cb` is destroyed
`1 0`, and the callback never runs because it was registered too late
questions.explanation: `request_stop` returns `true` only for the call that actually makes the stop request, so the second call returns `false`. A `stop_callback` constructed after stop has been requested invokes its callback immediately, in the constructing thread, before the constructor returns. That is why `callback` is printed first. A callback registered late is never lost, which rules out the first and last options.

questions.prompt: What does the standard guarantee about the value of `std::thread::hardware_concurrency()`?
options: It is at least 1, since the calling thread is running on some hardware context
It is the maximum number of `std::thread` objects that can be joinable at once
It equals the number of physical cores
It is a hint about hardware thread contexts, and may be 0 if not computable or not well defined
questions.explanation: [thread.thread.static] describes the value as the number of hardware thread contexts, to be regarded only as a hint, and says it returns 0 when the value is not computable or well defined. Nothing promises it is at least 1, so code that sizes a pool from it should clamp. It says nothing about how many threads may be created, and hardware thread contexts typically count simultaneous multithreading siblings, not physical cores.

questions.prompt: What is guaranteed to be printed?
options: `body`, `joined`, `dtor`: thread-local objects are destroyed at program exit
`body`, `dtor`, `joined`
`body` and `joined`, with `dtor` in an unspecified position
`body` and `joined` only: thread-local objects of other threads are never destroyed
questions.explanation: Constructed objects with thread storage duration are destroyed as a result of the thread returning from its initial function, per [basic.start.term], so their destruction is part of that thread's completion. [thread.thread.member] says the thread's completion synchronizes with the successful return of `join()`. So `dtor` is printed before `join` returns, and therefore before `joined`. The first option confuses thread storage with static storage, which is destroyed at program exit.
